preamble: Each across clue leads to one of a kind, undefined

parts.note: surface reading: some dwelling in a Berkshire village
setter's reading: the home of the famous clergyman of Bray, or of the TV clergywoman of Dibley

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Vicar of Bray' is an old song about a turncoat cleric; 'The Vicar of Dibley' is a British TV sitcom about a woman priest. Each vicar would live in the parish house.
explanation.definitionFit: The parish clergyman's official residence is named after his office, so it is the home of either famous vicar.

clue.text: A tailless donkey in a frenzy

indicators.note: an animal without its tail has lost its end, so the word's final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
moke is British slang for a donkey

explanation.surface: A donkey without a tail is running wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Moke is informal British slang for a donkey, little known outside the UK; 'tailless' is a common crossword way to drop a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to behave wildly and uncontrollably, the same state as being in a frenzy.

indicators.note: a baying pack is wild and noisy, so its letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An explorer travels by dog sled, the dogs howling as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed question tells you the hounds are wild, which is the cue to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Hudson was the English navigator who gave his name to Hudson Bay and the Hudson River.

clue.text: Turn round behind the Queen's Head

definitions.meaning: first meaning: go backwards or turn the other way
second meaning: the back face of a coin, opposite the side with the monarch's portrait

explanation.surface: Directions to a pub: turn back behind the Queen's Head.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's Head reads like a pub name; in fact it is the head on a British coin, whose back is called the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for going backwards and a noun for the tails side of a coin or medal.

parts.note: app. is an abbreviation of applied
a roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss saying that one word means 'applied to fish'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase looks like a definition of 'Means', but it is the wordplay: the abbreviation for applied set against a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An approach is a method or way of tackling something, as are means.

clue.text: Cuts of meat served with honour and pride

parts.note: a medal is an honour awarded
a pride is a group of lions

explanation.surface: A menu promising meat served with ceremony and dignity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' is a collective noun: the animals it names supply the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Medallions are small round slices of tender meat such as pork or beef fillet.

clue.text: Homer's gone astray after one of his letters

indicators.note: coming after means being placed later in the line than the other piece

parts.note: Homer wrote in Greek, and pi is a Greek letter

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so the order is lost and must be rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Greek poet has wandered off, lost after some letter of his.
explanation.walkthrough: Homer looks like the poet, and his letters are Greek ones; but the definition is a homer, a homing bird that should never go astray.
explanation.definitionFit: A homer is a homing pigeon, a bird trained to fly back to its loft from far away.

indicators.note: to sort things is to rearrange them into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says every across answer is a bird with no definition in the clue, so the whole clue is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A titmouse is a small songbird, the older full name for a tit, which fits the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: trimming the edges cuts away the ends of the phrase, leaving what sits inside

parts.note: the two words run together lose their first and last letters

explanation.surface: A fencing sword whose tip and guard have been filed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' looks like a link to the epee, but it is part of the string being trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: The peewit is the lapwing, a plover named for its call, so it suits the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: the head of anything is its top, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
the ark is Noah's vessel

explanation.surface: The captain or figurehead of a big ship.
explanation.walkthrough: With no definition in across clues, all three words build the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The lark is a songbird famed for singing while rising high, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: fluttering is restless flapping about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: nine letters, one short of the answer
nothing in the printed clue supplies the second R; the clue appears to have lost a word such as 'round', so it is supplied here

explanation.walkthrough: As printed the clue is one R short of the bird, likely a misprint. Wheatears are themselves birds, a playful decoy since the answer is a different bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A shearwater is a seabird that skims low over the waves, matching the preamble's bird theme.

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall, reaching the sea at Falmouth
a con is a swindle

explanation.surface: A swindle pulled on a river in Cornwall, the county at England's south-west tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Cornwall is a county at England's south-western tip; its river Fal gives the start of the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The falcon is a swift hunting bird of prey, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

clue.text: Playing around in cod Gluck composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, here by arranging letters afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone fooling about in a mock piece by the opera composer Gluck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link but joins the letters; 'cod' means mock, though here it is just more fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckolding is deceiving a spouse by sleeping with another, a sharper sense of the idiom playing around.

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit within it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a sling supports an injured arm
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman with his arm in a sling.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR, short for tarpaulin, is the classic crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The starling is a common speckled songbird known for vast flocks, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: something hollow has nothing inside, so only the outside letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
taken as written
a stopcock is a tap controlling flow

explanation.surface: A plumbing description: an empty pipe fitted with a tap.
explanation.walkthrough: A cock, as in stopcock, is a valve or tap.
explanation.definitionFit: The peacock is the male peafowl with its showy fanned tail, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

clue.text: Costumes fit for a Lloyd Webber musical?

definitions.text: Costumes fit for a Lloyd Webber musical?

parts.note: surface reading: outfits suitable for a stage show
setter's reading: Andrew Lloyd Webber's Cats, so the outfits are suits for cats

explanation.surface: Wardrobe planning for a West End show.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd Webber's best-known shows include Cats; outfits fit for that show are literally suits for cats.
explanation.definitionFit: A catsuit is a close-fitting one-piece garment covering body, arms and legs, worn as a costume.

parts.note: Doctor Who is the long-running BBC science-fiction series

indicators.note: a knotted line is twisted and tangled, so its letters are muddled up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The television time traveller holding a tangled rope.
explanation.walkthrough: The TV doctor is the Doctor of Doctor Who, giving just his show's last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The whooper is a large swan named for its loud call, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a piece of high or rising ground
second meaning: fame and superiority of rank

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as one idea, the peak of excellence, but splits into two meanings of the same noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names both a hill or raised ground and the condition of being renowned or eminent.

parts.note: surface reading: chief, fundamental, as in a cardinal rule
setter's reading: a quality of a cardinal, the churchman robed in scarlet or the scarlet bird

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal property' sounds like a key attribute, or a church estate; really it is the colour a cardinal is known for.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardinal's vestments are scarlet, so the quality belonging to one is being red.

indicators.note: placed after means it follows the other piece in the line

parts.note: the Model T was Henry Ford's famous car

indicators.note: something designed is newly shaped, so these letters are refashioned

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gun holster styled to match a Ford car.
explanation.walkthrough: Ford's best-known model was the Model T, so just its letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Throstle is an old and dialect name for the song thrush, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

parts.note: surface reading: a medical inhaler, or someone breathing steam
setter's reading: a Middle Eastern smoking device that draws smoke through a bowl of water

explanation.walkthrough: A Turkish bath suggests steam to breathe; the water-filled, Turkish-associated pipe is the thing you inhale through.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah is an oriental tobacco pipe whose smoke is cooled by passing through water before being drawn in.

indicators.note: sloppy means careless and messy, so the letters are left in disarray

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe marking the dropped letter

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe trims the word to exactly six letters for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The siskin is a small yellow-green finch, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

parts.note: surface reading: life is simple for wealthy people
setter's reading: 'easy' is the name of the place the prosperous are said to live on

explanation.walkthrough: To be 'on Easy Street' is an idiom for being well off, so the thing that is 'easy' for the rich is their road.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom Easy Street names a comfortable, wealthy life, so the answer is the road in that phrase.

parts.note: surface reading: a prostitute soliciting on the street
setter's reading: one moving along the highway at speed, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: 'Streetwalker' suggests a prostitute, but split it into its parts and speed it up: one who runs along the road.
explanation.definitionFit: The roadrunner is a fast-running ground cuckoo of the American south-west, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: a setback sends things backwards, so the word is read from the end
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within

parts.note: fresh means new
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A monarch suffering a fresh setback.
explanation.walkthrough: R, from Regina, is a standard abbreviation for the Queen; the ellipsis just joins this clue to the next two.
explanation.definitionFit: The wren is a tiny brown songbird with a cocked tail, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in cricket, a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, which counts as an extra run
second meaning: large from side to side

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it means very broad; split, 'Extra' is a cricket term for a run not scored off the bat, of which a badly aimed delivery is one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a delivery too far from the batsman is called this and gives a bonus run; the adjective also means of great breadth.

indicators.note: to be in something is to be held inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: GT, gran turismo, labels a sporty touring car
Anne is the British Princess Royal

explanation.surface: A royal driving a fast car, continuing the story of the Queen's troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Anne, the Queen's daughter, is the usual crossword princess.
explanation.definitionFit: The gannet is a large white diving seabird, fitting the preamble's bird theme.

indicators.note: being in something means lying inside it, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: to exhaust air is to draw it out, to suck
something caught is held

explanation.surface: The princess caught by a speed camera, or trapped in fumes, ending the royal saga.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' usually gives C in crosswords; here it is a whole word for being gripped.
explanation.definitionFit: The shelduck is a large boldly patterned duck of coasts and estuaries, fitting the preamble's bird theme.
